1.summary: Mayfair, Kensington and Chelsea have long been the stomping ground of the elite -- and are now welcoming a new wave of African investors. These investors mainly come from just six countries: Nigeria, Ghana, Congo, Gabon, Cameroon and Senegal. Nigerians are splashing out the most cash -- typically spending between $22 and $37 million on securing a property, according to luxury property agents Beauchamp Estates. Their research shows that over the past three years Africans have spent over $900 million on luxury residential property in London. High-end auction house Sotheby's says that foreign investors see London as a "safe haven" for prime property investments, and ranks the city as the second most important hub for ultra high-net-worth homes, behind New York City. As well as an intelligent investment, many of the African buyers see these houses as a way of maintaining long standing cultural ties with London -- and it's here they want to send their children to school. The Nigerian Embassy in London calculates that Nigerian nationals now spend over $446 million per year on fees, tutoring and accommodation at British schools and university. Education industry experts ICEF Monitor say there were over 17,500 Nigerians studying in British universities in 2012 -- about 1,000 more than the 2009/10 academic session. "Virtually all the transactions are for end use, not rental investment, which indicates that the African buyer market in London has significant room for growth," says Gary Hersham, director at Beauchamp Estates.

2.summary: Al Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula said senior leader Ibrahim al-Rubaish was one of five people killed in an airstrike in Yemen on Monday night. The group's media arm described him as both a religious scholar and a combat commander. Three Yemeni officials confirmed his death but could not establish how he was killed, leaving the circumstances uncertain. Al-Rubaish had previously been detained at Guantanamo Bay and challenged his confinement before being released through Saudi Arabia's rehabilitation program for jihadist terrorists. The United States had cooperated with Yemeni governments against AQAP, and drone attacks had killed other members, but the report did not establish that a drone killed al-Rubaish. Yemen's instability deepened after Houthi rebels captured Sanaa and forced President Abdu Rabu Mansour Hadi from office in January. Hadi continued to assert his legitimacy and worked with a Saudi-led coalition against the Houthis and supporters of former President Ali Abdullah Saleh. The disorder also created opportunities for AQAP: a senior Defense Ministry official said a prison escape earlier that month freed 270 inmates, including senior members of the group. The United States had withdrawn its remaining special operations personnel the previous month, a move some believed would further benefit AQAP.

3.summary: London (CNN)A Polish Prince has challenged populist British politician Nigel Farage to a duel in London's Hyde Park over his immigration policy. In a video posted on YouTube, Prince Jan Zylinski said he was fed up with discrimination against Poles living in Britain. Farage -- who is on the campaign trail ahead of Britain's general elections on May 7 -- said he did not intend to cross swords with the prince. "Alternatively, if you don't agree or if your sword is a little bit rusty, Mr. Farage, we can meet for a different kind of duel -- a duel with words in a TV studio in the run-up to the elections," Zylinski suggested.

4.summary: Hawaii is poised to become the first state in the nation to prohibit the sale of cigarettes and other tobacco products to anybody under age 21, after the state's legislature on Friday passed a bill raising the minimum legal age -- currently 18 -- to buy tobacco or e-cigarettes. The bill will now go before Gov. David Ige, whose signature would make it law in Hawaii as of January 1, 2016, but it was not clear Monday whether he would sign it. An Institute of Medicine report estimated that setting the minimum age at 21 nationwide would result in nearly a quarter-million fewer premature deaths and 50,000 fewer deaths from lung cancer among people born between 2000 and 2019. Under the Hawaii bill, anyone caught breaking the law would face a $10 fine for the first offense and a $50 fine or community service for a second offense.

5.summary: Julian Assange agreed to questioning by Swedish prosecutors at Ecuador's London embassy over 2010 rape and molestation allegations, his lawyer said, although British and Ecuadorian permission is still needed. Prosecutors changed their approach because some alleged offenses face an August 2015 limitation deadline; Assange has not been charged and denies the allegations.

Julian Assange's Swedish lawyer said the WikiLeaks founder agreed to questioning by Swedish prosecutors at London's Ecuadorian Embassy about allegations of rape and sexual molestation from 2010; Assange has not been charged and denies the claims. His lawyer said British and Ecuadorian permission would be needed, while prosecutors reversed their refusal to travel because the limitation period for some alleged crimes expires in August 2015.

Julian Assange, who denies the 2010 rape and molestation allegations and has not been charged, has agreed to questioning by Swedish prosecutors in London, his lawyer said. Prosecutors changed their position as some alleged crimes approach the August 2015 statute-of-limitations deadline, but must still seek British and Ecuadorian permission to interview him at the Ecuadorian Embassy, where he has stayed since June 2012 to avoid extradition to Sweden.
